analysis.one_liner: Creates an old-growth forest reserve in the Pacific Northwest while guaranteeing annual federal timber sales and limiting court challenges.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 19 cosponsors from both parties and two subcommittee hearings, but the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee never voted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up an Old Growth Forest Reserve on federal lands in Oregon, Washington, and Northern California to protect the Northern Spotted Owl and old-growth habitat, with new mining barred inside it. At the same time, it would have guaranteed minimum annual timber sales from those same lands regardless of any court order, made the adopted plans enough to satisfy endangered-species law until revision, and sharply limited who can challenge logging in court and how fast they must act. It also set up a fund, paid from federal timber receipts, for retraining, income support, and aid to timber towns.
analysis.who_benefits: Pacific Northwest timber towns and displaced mill workers would get retraining, extended income support, and health coverage paid from a federal timber-receipt fund. Old-growth forest and the Northern Spotted Owl would get a statutory reserve on federal, state, and park lands. Timber mills would get a guaranteed annual supply of federal timber that courts could not shut down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owls, old growth, timber towns, and mills

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Old Growth Forest Reserve protecting ecologically significant old-growth forest and the Northern Spotted Owl on federal and, by governor petition, state lands in Oregon, Washington, and Northern California.
Closes reserve areas to new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing.

Provides timber workers with retraining, extended income support, base health coverage, and relocation aid, and provides grants to help timber-dependent communities diversify, funded from federal timber receipts.
Allows roads, recreation, hunting, trapping, and fishing in the reserve where consistent with its protection.
Requires economic-impact analyses for timber-dependent communities and phases in any output change greater than 10 percent per year over four years to avoid abrupt job losses.
Guarantees a minimum decadal level of timber sale volume from each planning area, with at least 25 percent offered in any three consecutive years.

analysis.who_pays: Citizens who want to challenge logging or road-building in court would face short filing deadlines, limited standing to sue, no injunctions after 60 days, and a requirement to exhaust administrative appeals first. Some old-growth outside the reserve would stay open to logging under guaranteed sale levels, and endangered-species obligations would be considered discharged once a plan is adopted, until it is revised.
analysis.who_pays_short: Citizens challenging logging, and owls' habitat outside the reserve

drawbacks.text: The interim timber program requires sales 'notwithstanding any provision of law or order of a court to the contrary,' overriding existing court orders protecting spotted owl habitat.
Challenges to interim timber programs must be filed in the Ninth Circuit within 30 days, no injunction can issue after 60 days, and grounds are limited to compliance with the act itself.
Standing to appeal or sue over forest plans is limited to people who commented during planning, with 60-, 90-, and 30-day deadlines and mandatory administrative exhaustion that cut off later review.

Once a land management plan completes Endangered Species Act consultation, federal responsibilities for the owl and old-growth species are declared 'fully discharged' until the plan is revised or significantly amended.

The strongest good-faith case for these limits was that appeals and litigation had repeatedly blocked forest plans and forced emergency congressional action, and that timber communities needed certainty; the acknowledged cost is that the same provisions would shut ordinary citizens and conservation groups out of the courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reserve and the worker aid were genuine, and the bill tried to buy habitat protection by paying timber communities and guaranteeing mills a supply. But the price was steep: it overrode court orders, declared endangered-species duties discharged at plan adoption, and imposed some of the tightest litigation limits Congress had proposed on this issue. A reader can fairly see it as a real compromise or as trading enforceable species protection for a litigation shield for logging; the design heavily favored continued timber output.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which passed it to its public lands subcommittee and held hearings in 1991 and 1992 but never voted to report it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Packwood introduced the bill on May 23, 1991, joined by original cosponsors including Sens. Hatfield, Gorton, Murkowski, Breaux, Heflin, and Shelby.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, then to its Subcommittee on Public Lands, National Parks.
The committee requested executive comments from the Departments of Agriculture, Labor, and Justice and from OMB in July 1991.
The subcommittee held hearings in August 1991 (S.Hrg. 102-286) and again in July 1992 (S.Hrg. 102-980).
No committee vote, Senate floor action, or House action ever followed, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, conservation groups kept their full ability to appeal and litigate timber sales in court, and the timber industry gained no court-proof guaranteed harvest levels; but timber towns also got none of the promised worker aid, and the spotted owl dispute stayed stuck in the courts until later outside this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Court-challengers of logging kept their tools

industries.note: The bill would have locked in a guaranteed minimum annual federal timber supply offered regardless of court orders, with phase-in limits and decadal sale floors, while also restricting the reserve's boundaries to designated old growth. It regulated the industry's access but made federal timber a permanent, court-proof input for mills.

A dedicated fund from federal timber receipts would pay retraining, extended income support, health coverage, relocation aid, and community diversification grants — ordinary workers and towns are the direct beneficiaries of Title IV.

Standing limits, mandatory petitions instead of appeals, 30- to 90-day filing windows, and bans on injunctions would have sharply curtailed the legal tools citizens and conservation groups used to challenge federal logging, which the bill's own findings describe as having repeatedly delayed timber sales.

Reserve lands would be withdrawn from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, and interim restrictions would block leasing near owl nest sites, ending industry access to those areas.
The bill expressly permits motorized and nonmotorized access, recreation, hunting, trapping, and fishing in the reserve, preserving public use of protected lands.
